header.tag_why: The rep says it was a bake-off until a customer engineer used our docs and sandbox to build a working sitter payment flow over a weekend, and after that Daniel 'stopped saying' if; marketplace onboarding and local-currency sitter pay is the close second.

evidence.excerpt: Expansion. They were launching Canada, then the UK, and sitters have to get paid locally.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: a haunted house.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Two engineers more or less full-time just keeping sitter payments working.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: There was also a roadmap item, faster pay for sitters, that had been pushed three quarters in a row.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: Expansion set the timing, but the pain was engineering toil: two engineers tied up keeping sitter pay running, and a faster-pay feature that kept slipping. Our 'grow globally, in every currency' opener (M1) speaks only to the timing and misses the reason a VP of Engineering wanted to rip out the code.
trigger.messaging: For marketplace buyers led by engineering, open with getting engineers off payments maintenance and shipping faster sitter pay, and treat new-country payouts as the proof rather than the headline.

evidence.excerpt: Daniel. He signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this is an engineering decision, finance will sign what I bring them.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: does this change when sitters get paid?
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: Daniel decided and finance rubber-stamped, so ROI framing (M6) had no audience here. The CFO's only question was about when sitters get paid, not cost. That is a sign sitter-pay timing is the business-critical promise even for finance. The rep's own wrap-up suggests a customer engineer was the real influencer below Daniel, and the decider answer doesn't capture that.
decider.messaging: Arm the engineering decider to carry the deal, and prepare a one-line answer for finance on sitter pay timing ('paid by Friday') rather than an ROI deck.

evidence.excerpt: I've stopped learning their names.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Do we lose PayPal, do we lose Venmo, what happens to the saved cards.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I assume Braintree told them they'd lose things.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: They had a call with Braintree in the middle of the evaluation.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: The customer raised two things: account-manager churn and fear of losing the PayPal and Venmo buttons. Their questions then moved from build speed to loss: PayPal, Venmo, saved cards. The rep only infers the Braintree call from that shift, and what Braintree said is a guess. It is also never stated whether Braintree was the incumbent, although talk of moving saved cards points to an existing provider.
competitor.messaging: Answer 'what do we lose' before the competitor frames it: spell out what stays (PayPal, Venmo), how saved cards move, and who the customer's named contact is.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the docs and the sandbox.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And the marketplace piece.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence: the acceptance-rate slide.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M2 (developers) and M11 (sitter onboarding, identity checks, local-currency payouts) landed. M4's average-uplift claim fell flat because it ignored the customer's own economics: at a 38-dollar booking, the decider didn't care. The rep presented a generic average slide instead of testing whether acceptance mattered to this buyer.
message.messaging: For low-ticket marketplaces, cut the acceptance-rate slide and spend that time on a sandbox walkthrough of a sitter pay flow.

evidence.excerpt: One of their engineers, on her own time, built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend and showed it at Monday standup.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before that it was a bake-off. After that Daniel stopped saying
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't even know until Daniel told me.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Only that I barely sold this. Their engineer did.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The turning point was a working prototype that the customer built on their own time, and the rep didn't know it was happening. That makes the win real but accidental. We can't repeat it unless we deliberately give engineers a reason and a path to build during the evaluation.
decided.messaging: Make 'a working sitter pay flow in a weekend' a deliberate step in the evaluation: offer a starter sitter-payout sandbox project and invite the team to show it at standup.

evidence.excerpt: Nothing, really. It was a clean one.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: I didn't have a crisp answer on Venmo in the room, and I still don't.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: who's done this at our size without losing cards?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we'll find out.
evidence.label: quote

gaps.insight: It was not clean. The PayPal answer was put off to implementation, Venmo is still unanswered, and Daniel's request for a peer reference on saved-card migration was never answered. A customer engineer said 'we'll find out' at kickoff, so the risk moved into implementation rather than going away. We have no customer story (M8) for card migration at their size, and that is exactly the proof the competitor's framing exploits.
gaps.messaging: Build a saved-card migration reference and a written PayPal/Venmo coexistence answer before claiming switching is painless.

evidence.excerpt: a haunted house.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Payments shouldn't be a team
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We want to stop babysitting this.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: And nobody says 'payouts.' They say 'sitter pay.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: They describe the problem as a burden on engineers ('haunted house', 'babysitting') and a promise to sitters ('paid by Friday'). Our words 'marketplace', 'payouts' and 'financial infrastructure' are not theirs; they say 'the app' and 'sitter pay'.
language.messaging: Use their framing: 'Payments shouldn't be a team.' Stop babysitting sitter pay and keep 'paid by Friday' in every new country.

gaps.question: What was the deal size (ACV)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya for the signed annual contract value.

gaps.question: What did they use before, and was Braintree the incumbent?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya (or Daniel) who processed payments before and whose account manager changed three times.

gaps.question: What did Braintree tell them on that mid-evaluation call?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel what Braintree said about losing PayPal, Venmo or saved cards.

gaps.question: What did they ask for that we couldn't show?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the product team for a definitive Venmo answer, and have Priya send it to Daniel before implementation goes further.

gaps.question: Who has migrated saved cards at their size without losing any?
gaps.follow_up: Priya should get a reference customer from customer success now and send it to Daniel and his engineer before cutover.

gaps.question: What made the engineer build the weekend prototype?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel (or the engineer) what prompted her to build it and which docs or sandbox parts she used.

close.rep_takeaway: A deal you call 'clean' can still carry open promises. Close every 'I'll get back to you' (the Venmo answer, the saved-card reference) before kickoff. And when the customer's engineers start building, find out early and back them, because that is where this deal was won.
